This section opens Steven Pinker’s unromantic theory of the emotions, arguing that emotions are not unruly animal remnants but well-engineered computational modules that set an organism’s highest-level goals and work with intellect (file page 217). He rejects Paul MacLean’s Triune Brain: evolution modifies existing circuitry rather than stacking untouched layers, emotional software varies across species, sex, age, and breeds, and the amygdala exchanges two-way signals with the cortex, so emotion can be triggered by abstract appraisals like a Dear John letter or an ambulance in the driveway (file pages 217–218).

Pinker’s reasoning begins with a thought experiment: an emotionless Mr. Spock would still need curiosity, goals, and fear to direct his faculties, because intelligence is goal pursuit under obstacles and is meaningless without goals (file pages 218–219). Means–ends reasoning nests subgoals, as in reaching a locked apartment through pliers and a store, but the topmost goal comes from the programmer in artificial intelligence and from natural selection in organisms (file page 219). Because an animal cannot pursue all goals at once, emotions commit the body to one goal at the right moment; fear, for example, prioritizes escape, future avoidance, and remembering the successful route, while also preparing the body for any time-sensitive action (file pages 219–220). Pinker notes that most artificial intelligence researchers expect freely behaving robots to need something like emotions to decide what to do next, while leaving robot sentience as a separate question (file page 219).

The chapter then turns to emotions about physical environments. Drawing on Cosmides and Tooby, Pinker likens ancestral life to a lifelong camping trip requiring mechanisms that prefer habitats supplying food, water, shelter, information, and safety (file page 220). Humans are adapted to the African savanna and, aided by intellect, mapped and even remade new lands into savanna-like terrain (file pages 220–221). Experiments show children preferring savannas despite never visiting one, while adults also like familiar forests; Orians, Heerwagen, and the Kaplans interpret beauty as a habitat-selection mechanism favoring semi-open space, views, trees, water, and prospect and refuge (file pages 220–221). Landscapes must also be legible through landmarks and reference frames, and “mystery” in paths and partial views invites exploration (file page 221). Flowers attract us as diagnostic plant signals and harbingers of future food, while sunsets, storms, and fire arrest attention because they announce consequential change (file page 221).

Finally, disgust illustrates emotion’s independence from literal rationality. It is universal, tenacious, and directed at incorporating animal substances into the body; sterilized cockroaches, clean urine bottles, and feces-shaped fudge remain revolting, and Western aversions to nutritious insects resist sanitary or gustatory explanations (file pages 221–222). Paul Rozin characterizes disgust as fear of incorporation, expressed by spitting, vomiting, and a nose-wrinkling, tongue-protruding face; its objects are chiefly animals, animal parts, and body products, especially feces and decay, whereas plant dislikes are mere distaste (file page 222).

Engineering implications, distinct from Pinker’s claims: a thinking machine could implement emotions as priority-setting mechanisms that select among competing goals, trigger nested subgoal stacks, and modulate memory encoding and bodily readiness. Habitat aesthetics suggests representational features for prospect, refuge, legibility, and mystery; disgust suggests category-sensitive evaluators whose judgments can override surface plausibility. None of this demonstrates human intelligence or consciousness, and the excerpt leaves unsolved how grounded concepts, learning, and generalization are built.
